roof_form.note: Deliberately left open. Craftsman, California Bungalow and Craftsman Bungalow are canonically gabled; Prairie School is canonically hipped and its own hard constraint (prairie-school.c01) forbids a gabled principal roof outright. This is the single largest real disagreement inside the family -- see roof_pitch, which IS shared, for the trait that survives the split.

roof_pitch.rule: Roof pitch stays low across the whole family, 3:12 to 6:12 -- never a steep or vertical reading -- which is what lets the deep eave register as a plane rather than a gesture.
roof_pitch.note: Synthesized from the members' own documented ranges: arts-and-crafts-american 4:12-6:12, craftsman 3:12-6:12, prairie-school 3:12-4:12, california-bungalow 3:12-5:12, craftsman-bungalow 4:12-6:12. The union is 3:12-6:12; every member's own band sits inside it. ROOF FORM (gable vs hip) is the family's real internal split and is left open at composition below -- pitch is shared, form is not.

variants.note: Canonical in the Craftsman lineage (arts-and-crafts-american, craftsman, california-bungalow, craftsman-bungalow all name exposed, shaped rafter tails and knee braces as a defining or diagnostic trait).
Canonical in Prairie School, whose own diagnostic_tells state 'the eave soffit is clean: no rafter tails, no knee braces, no brackets' and whose c02 forbids exposed structure outright.

projection_in.note: Union of the members' own stated eave/rake bands (24-36 in for the Craftsman lineage, 30-48 in for Prairie and California Bungalow).

eave_condition.rule: The eave projects deep enough to throw the wall into shadow for most of the day across every branch of the family; whether the soffit displays the rafters (Craftsman lineage) or closes into one unbroken plane (Prairie) is the family's principal internal branch point and is deliberately not resolved here.

variants.note: The dominant technology across the family's whole floruit (1900-1935), spanning the transition from balloon to platform framing.

No member's exemplars are load-bearing masonry; masonry throughout the family is reserved for piers, foundations and chimneys, never the primary wall. A masonry bearing wall belongs to Georgian or Colonial Revival, not to this family.
Same reasoning as solid-masonry-two-wythe: no member's exemplars are load-bearing masonry.

construction_type.rule: The primary structure is wood frame; masonry is reserved for bases, piers, foundations and chimneys and never carries the wall as a bearing material.
construction_type.note: Not explicitly stated as 'construction_type' by name in any member's own text -- inferred from the fact that every exemplar across all five member nodes (Gamble House, Craftsman Farms, Bungalow Heaven, Robie House, Sears kit houses) is wood-frame with masonry accents only, and none is described as a bearing-masonry building. Marked judgment because it is an inference from consistent absence rather than a documented statement.

material_change_rule.rule: No more than three wall materials per elevation, each change occurring only at a real structural line -- water table, belt, plate, or gable line -- and returning fully around any corner it meets.
material_change_rule.note: Directly and repeatedly documented: arts-and-crafts-american's own hard constraint (c05) states this almost verbatim; craftsman's defining_characteristics state 'stacked natural materials expressing base, wall, and gable, with each transition at a structural line'; california-bungalow repeats the same principle. Not found stated for prairie-school specifically, but prairie's own wall treatment (continuous stucco or Roman brick, rarely stacked) does not contradict the rule -- it simply exercises the single-material end of it.

corner_quoin.rule: Quoins are a classical masonry-order device and are incompatible with a family whose whole argument is that ornament must be produced by construction rather than applied from a pattern-book vocabulary.
corner_quoin.note: Not separately discussed in any member's own text -- no member ever shows a quoined corner in its exemplars or diagnostic_tells -- but this follows directly from the family-wide classical-apparatus prohibition below and the general 'ornament must arise from construction' rule that is this family's own stated defining content.

variants.note: Wide, flat, unmoulded -- matches the family's own repeated diagnostic of 'wide flat unpainted trim.'
Common where board-and-batten cladding is used, especially in the California branch.
A classical device; see the family-wide classical-apparatus prohibition.

corner_board.rule: The corner is a plain, flat board sized to the trim it terminates, never a classical pilaster or moulded backband.
corner_board.note: Inferred from the family's repeated 'wide flat trim' diagnostic (arts-and-crafts-american, craftsman-bungalow) rather than a slot the members discuss by name.

color_strategy.rule: Materials are left in their own colour and texture -- unpainted or matte-stained wood, clinker brick, river rock, stucco, matte tile -- never painted white or high-gloss; the reform argument is that a material honestly shown does not need a coat to explain it.
color_strategy.note: AAC's own defining_characteristics states this almost word for word ('Materials left in their own colour and texture: unpainted or matte-stained wood...'); craftsman's long description states flatly 'Nothing is painted white.' Not separately restated for Prairie or the two variants, but nothing in their own texts contradicts it and Prairie's stucco-and-Roman-brick palette is consistent with the same ethic.

variants.note: A classical device; see the family-wide classical-apparatus prohibition.

window_head_wood.rule: Window heads are flat, wide, and unmoulded or lightly moulded -- never a pedimented or cornice head, which would import a classical order this family explicitly rejects.
window_head_wood.note: No member states a window-head profile explicitly; this follows from the family's repeated 'wide flat trim, no applied classical ornament' rule (arts-and-crafts-american c03, craftsman distinguished_from colonial-revival) rather than a directly documented figure. Left open for window_head_masonry, since solid masonry bearing walls are themselves forbidden at construction_type and a masonry window head is largely moot for this family.

variants.note: A classical device; see the family-wide classical-apparatus prohibition.

window_surround_wood.rule: The surround is flat, wide casing, not a classical architrave with ears or a pilastered entablature.
window_surround_wood.note: Follows the same 'wide flat unpainted trim' diagnostic used across the family rather than a member text naming this slot directly.

variants.note: A Tudor/English Arts and Crafts device, not the American movement's own vocabulary; the American branch's art glass is rectilinear, not diamond-paned.

special_window.rule: Art glass, where used, is rectilinear and geometric -- never floral, curvilinear, or diamond-leaded -- and its pattern is derived from the building's own structural geometry rather than borrowed from a decorative catalogue.
special_window.note: Directly stated for arts-and-crafts-american (diagnostic_tells: 'Art glass in rectilinear, non-floral geometry') and for prairie-school (long description: 'rectilinear geometry and no curves'; diagnostic_tells: 'no curves'). Not separately emphasized in craftsman's or the two bungalow variants' own texts, but nothing in them contradicts it.

order.rule: No classical order is used anywhere in the family; a column is a post, sized by the load and the batter, not by a module derived from a Tuscan or Corinthian diameter.
order.note: The whole classical-apparatus group is forbidden at the family level. This is not an inference: arts-and-crafts-american's own hard constraint (c03) forbids applied classical orders outright; craftsman's own distinguished_from entry against colonial-revival states it 'has no orders at all'; prairie-school's own hard constraint (c02) forbids 'any classical or revival ornament.' All three direct style children and both variants (which inherit the craftsman prohibition) agree. This mirrors the precedent docs/inheritance.md itself gives for family-level classical-apparatus prohibition (Prairie forbidding 'most of the classical apparatus outright').

column.rule: Porch supports are square posts or battered piers, never a turned, fluted, or entasis-bearing classical column.

entablature.rule: No engaged classical entablature is built; where a cornice or frieze occurs it is a carpenter's or mason's construction detail, not the base-shaft-cap logic of an order.

pediment.rule: No pediment, triangular or otherwise, appears over an opening or a portico; a gable is a roof shape, not a pediment quoting a temple front.

pilaster.rule: No pilaster is applied to a wall or a corner; where the wall needs a vertical stop it is a plain post or board, never a flattened classical column.

modillion_dentil.rule: No modillion or dentil course appears anywhere in the family; a cornice, where one exists, is a plain board or a bracket run, never a run of classical blocks.

balustrade.rule: No turned classical balustrade appears at a porch, stair, or roof edge; a rail, where used, is a simple square or battered picket, not a run of classical balusters.

ornament_vocabulary.rule: No classical ornament vocabulary -- swag-and-urn, guttae-triglyph, acanthus, fan-and-patera -- is used anywhere in the family; ornament, where it exists at all, is the structure itself (a joint, a bracket, a rafter end) left visible, not an applied classical motif.

trim_family.rule: One coherent interior trim family: flat, wide, unmoulded or lightly moulded boards, in the wood's own colour, with a picture rail as the room's organizing datum rather than a classical crown. No classical profile family is mixed in.
trim_family.note: Directly grounded: craftsman's and craftsman-bungalow's own proportion_packs cite the trim-craftsman pack as close to a primary source, describing 'the picture rail as the room's datum' and 'the three-board casing family.' arts-and-crafts-american binds the same pack for the same reason. Prairie School binds trim-craftsman only 'optional' and with an explicit caveat that Wright's own bespoke geometric oak trim is a real gap the pack doesn't capture -- but Prairie's own trim ethic (geometric, non-classical, catalog-adjacent in its plan-book 'Prairie box' form) does not contradict the flat-unmoulded rule, it simply executes it more severely.

width_in.note: Drawn directly from craftsman-bungalow's own diagnostic tell: 'a wide flat casing 4 to 5 in deep around every opening.'

casing.rule: Casing is flat stock, 4 to 5 in wide, with little or no back-band, sized like a board rather than derived from an order.

crown.rule: A sprung classical crown moulding is forbidden; the picture rail, not a crown, is the room's upper datum.
crown.note: Directly quoted from craftsman's own proportion_packs note: 'the explicit prohibition on a mitred casing or a sprung classical crown that the movement was founded to object to.'

built_ins.rule: Built-in cabinetry -- bookcases flanking the hearth, a dining buffet, a window seat, a plate rail -- is original fabric that fixes the plan against rearrangement, not an optional upgrade added after the design is otherwise complete.
built_ins.note: One of the most repeatedly and explicitly documented traits in the whole family: arts-and-crafts-american's defining_characteristics ('built-in cabinetry replacing movable furniture'), craftsman's defining_characteristics ('built-in seating and cabinetry fixing the plan against rearrangement'), craftsman-bungalow's own hard constraint (c05, 'the hearth and its flanking built-ins must occupy a full wall'), and prairie-school's shared lineage note that it inherits 'the built-in furniture' from the same reform ethic.

variants.note: The formal parlour this family's whole reform programme was organized to eliminate.

circulation_parti.rule: The formal parlour is eliminated; circulation opens around a hearth-centred living space rather than through a sequence of closed, single-purpose rooms.
circulation_parti.note: arts-and-crafts-american: 'reorganized the middle-class plan around an open hearth-centred living room' and 'the open living room with built-in cabinetry...replacing fewer rooms'; craftsman-bungalow's own diagnostic tell: 'front door opens directly into the living room with no vestibule'; prairie-school's own lineage text: Wright's programme was to 'eliminate...the room-by-room subdivision of the ground floor.' Convergent across all three direct style children independently.

landscape_idiom.rule: House, interior fittings, furniture, and garden are conceived as one commission under one grammar; the landscape is not a separate decorative layer added after the building is finished.
landscape_idiom.note: AAC's own defining_characteristics states this directly ('House, interior fittings, furniture, and garden conceived as one commission under one grammar'), reinforced by the Gamble House and Craftsman Farms exemplars (whole-commission design) and by the California Bungalow's bungalow-court type, which is explicitly a landscape-and-massing move at once. Marked editorial because no member gives a dimensional or plant-list specification -- the claim is about design authorship, not a measurable rule.
